We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

item.title: A Catalytic Algorithm for Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries with Tight Query Bounds
item.dc:creator: Yu-Ao Chen
item.description:
Formalizes the paper's exact results (Secs. S1–S5: catalytic transposition circuit, query lower bounds, repeated-use constructions) in Lean 4 with Mathlib, provided as ancillary sources.
We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary $U\in\mathrm{SU}(3)$ using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements $m$ transpositions or inversions with $3+4m$ or $3+8m$ total queries, respectively. More generally, we prove that exact transposition and inversion of an unknown $U\in\mathrm{SU}(d)$, $d\ge2$, require at least $d+1$ and $d^2-1$ processing queries, respectively, in fixed causal order. These processing bounds hold for any program state prepared independently of the input state using finitely many forward queries, even if that state is consumed during processing. Both our catalytic qutrit algorithms attain their respective bounds. Moreover, exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries requires at least three preparation queries, and our construction attains this bound.

item.title: On the Five-Point Case of Mordell's Problem
item.dc:creator: Tiancheng Xu, Guowei Dou, Wensheng Yu
item.description:
The five-point Mordell discriminant inequality and both directions of its equality case are fully formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, including verified interval-bound checks.
For five complex points $z_1,\ldots,z_5$ satisfying $\sum_i|z_i|^2=5$, Mordell's discriminant inequality states that $\prod_{i<j}|z_i-z_j|^2\leq5^5$, with equality precisely for a unit regular pentagon, up to rotation and permutation. We organize its proof around a direct comparison of discriminant values. A global maximizer gives a centered stationary configuration, whose coefficient equations reduce the generic case to two quartic branches. On each branch, the absolute value of a cubic polynomial gives the original discriminant objective after accounting for the normalization scale. Exact rational interval bounds exclude both branches from the maximum, and the exceptional coefficient cases leave the regular pentagon. The argument determines the maximizing configuration without reconstructing all stationary shapes. We have completed a full Lean formalization of the five-point inequality and both directions of its equality condition, including all reductions and finite checks used in this proof.

item.title: Codimension-one holomorphic Anosov diffeomorphisms
item.dc:creator: Jiesong Zhang
item.description:
The main theorems and the Ghys results they rely on were formalised in Lean by a Peking University team using the SHEAF formalisation agent.
We prove that every codimension-one holomorphic Anosov diffeomorphism of a compact connected complex manifold is biholomorphically conjugate to a hyperbolic automorphism of a complex torus. This verifies a conjecture of Ghys in the codimension-one case and, in particular, in complex dimension three.

item.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
item.dc:creator: Anna Mei, Michael R. Douglas
item.description:
Builds an agentic Lean autoformalization pipeline for the NIST DLMF and verifies Lean statements using LLM semantic review, numerical checks, and vacuity checks.
We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF-Ch7ErrFunc-Release.git.

item.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
item.dc:creator: Jiatong Li, Yatao Bian
item.description:
Implements a Lean kernel that checks molecular state transitions and structural assertions for LLM chemical reasoning, with Lean-proved soundness of valence and connectivity validation.
Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

item.title: Generation by lazy and invertible cellular automata over the Klein four-group
item.dc:creator: Edgar Alcalá-Arroyo, Alonso Castillo-Ramirez, Haobo Ma, Wenlin Zhang
item.description:
The membership criterion and the cardinalities 59,712 and 4,007 are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, kernel-checked without native_decide, in supplementary material.
Let $G=C_2\times C_2$ and $A=\{0,1\}$. We characterize the submonoid of $\text{CA}(G;A)$ generated by lazy and invertible cellular automata. A cellular automaton belongs to this submonoid if and only if, whenever it maps the two free $G$-orbits onto the same free orbit, it maps both constant configurations and some two-point orbit to the same constant. The proof gives a factorization using elementary orbit collapses and three two-cell lazy maps. The criterion yields the cardinality $59\,712$ and identifies the maps missed by a weaker constant-separation invariant. Adjoining one idempotent generates the full monoid, and the generated submonoid is contained in exactly one maximal proper submonoid, of cardinality $65\,024$. The submonoid generated by lazy maps alone has $4\,007$ elements, and for both generating sets the maximum shortest-word length is six. The criterion and the cardinalities $59\,712$ and $4\,007$ are formally verified in Lean.

item.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu
item.description:
Formalizes the external-memory sorting theorem (correctness and I/O bounds) and the network-coding counterexample in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with a public repository.
Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem. We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $Θ(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.
